the effective shear viscosity in the quark-gluon plasma is bounded from below by the microscopic shear viscosity, and that second-order viscous hydrodynamical equations are inconsistent at low frequency if the shear viscosity is small enough.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the properties of a fluid, in this case the quark-gluon plasma, in the presence of a magnetic field.
the study of the hydrodynamical behavior of a system of strongly interacting particles.
the study of transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) in the framework of relativistic viscous fluid dynamics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

(a) the shear viscosity is bounded from above and below, with the upper bound being the microscopic value and the lower bound being set by the thermal fluctuations; (b) the second-order transport coefficients are divergent in the long wavelength limit, which means that hydrodynamics breaks down in that limit.
the shear viscosity of the QGP is bounded by 0.08 < η/s < 0.16.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the breakdown of second-order hydrodynamics is a real effect, but it is unlikely to affect the description of the Quark-Gloun Plasma.
we have derived a new absolute lower limit on the shear viscosity, and have found that the effective infrared shear viscosity is not much larger than the microscopic one.
the effective viscosity of the QGP is bounded from below by ηeff/s > 0.08, which is a factor of two larger than the bound obtained from the most recent lattice results.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effective shear viscosity in the infrared can be much larger than the microscopic shear viscosity, which may have important implications for the interpretation of heavy-ion collision data.
the breakdown scale of hydrodynamics is set not by the microscopic transport coefficients but by the scale at which the sound and shear waves are long lived.
the breakdown of viscous hydrodynamical behavior is not due to any particular transport coefficient, but rather to the breakdown of hydrodynamics itself.
